before: count++ reads, adds, and writes; two workers can read the same old value and lose one increment. A thread-safe task scheduler does not make every shared variable safe.

Enumerable.Range(0, 4) produces four integers. Select calls Task.Run once per integer; Task.Run queues the lambda on the thread pool. The unused lambda parameter is named _. ToArray enumerates the query now, so all four task objects are created before WhenAll.
lock(gate) allows one worker at a time into the protected block for that same gate. Every access that needs this protection must use the same gate.
The example creates one local gate object before starting workers. Creating a different gate inside each worker would provide no mutual exclusion between them. Do not await inside a lock body.
Expected behavior from this example: 4000 after all workers finish. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer: Replace the lock-protected increment with Interlocked.Increment after consulting its documentation. Explain why observed success without a lock would not prove safety. This is a separate local practice task, not a requirement to mark the reading complete.
after: count++ reads the old value, adds one, then writes it back. If workers overlap those steps, they can both read the same old value and lose an update.

Range supplies four values. For each one, Task.Run queues work on the thread pool, a set of threads that run queued jobs. ToArray reads the query now, creating all four tasks. The _ parameter is unused here.
lock(gate) lets only one worker at a time enter code protected by that same gate object. This keeps each read-add-write update together.
WhenAll waits for the workers before the final print. Each worker adds one a thousand times. The shared gate was created before any workers started.
The program prints 4000 after the four workers finish. The shared lock protects all four thousand updates.

A different gate in every worker would not make them take turns with each other. Updates could be lost even if some runs look correct. Keep the protected block short; C# does not allow await inside a lock block.

before.question: Move object gate = new() inside each worker. Which guarantee is lost?
choices: That all increments share one mutual-exclusion lock
before.explanation: Each worker would lock a different object. Its lock would no longer exclude the other workers, so lost updates become possible, not inevitable in every run.

after.question: Create a separate gate inside each worker. What protection is lost?
choices: All workers taking turns through the same lock
The ability for tasks to finish
The ability for an int to hold 4000
after.explanation: Different gate objects do not exclude the other workers. Their updates could overlap.
